{"notes": "Visit 1 (0:00-0:30). Plan: Maya proposed a fish (nose start, top and belly lines, forked tail) and assigned Tom top line, Priya bottom, Leo tail. Leo agreed, said he'd put the sketch up, but then swapped roles (Maya top, Tom bottom, Leo checks tail), which created some confusion about who owns what. Table at 0:30: one connected line of about 9 dominoes running from start diagonally down-right to around (7,13). No fork, no second line, no tail yet. Nothing pale/disconnected visible.

Maya: Fast to set direction and delegate clearly, good leadership signal so far. Sketching, but I don't know who placed the dominoes. Not yet any evidence on execution.

Tom: Assigned top line by Maya, then bottom line by Leo. Said nothing while I was there. No observed contribution yet; watch which line he takes and whether he builds.

Priya: Assigned bottom line by Maya, then dropped from Leo's reassignment. Silent while I was there. Nothing observed; she may be sidelined. Ask her privately how it's going.

Leo: Supported the plan quickly and took the sketch, but his re-assignment overrode Maya's and left Priya without a job. Mildly mixed on collaboration. Tail ownership unclear.

To check next visit: is the line branching into top/belly lines, who is actually building, whether Priya is included, whether the roles got sorted out, and any connection breaks. Don't rate anyone yet on attribution I can't verify."}

The top line has a short doubled, overlapping stretch around x=9-10, y=5.5-6.5, probably two people's work colliding. It's a redundant track and a possible misfire risk when pushed. The top line has not reached the tail junction, and there is no upper fork yet. The picture shows no hand labels, so I still can't say who placed what. I'm not scoring anyone on attribution I can't verify.

Maya: Stayed in charge. At 2:15 she gave a clear plan: Priya keeps going, she jumps to the middle of the back and meets her in between. Jumping ahead and meeting in the middle is a sound way to speed things up. Her role is still the strongest evidence for leadership. The doubled stretch may be where the segments met, but I can't confirm it was her. Execution is unverified.

Tom: Silent again and not mentioned in any instruction. I don't know what he's building. The bottom line is long and clean, but I can't credit him for it. Ask him directly, and ask the team privately who built it.

Priya: Now apparently on the top line, per Leo and Maya, so she is included again. Still silent to me. Ask her privately about the overlap and how she feels about the changing roles.

Leo: Coordinating from the side. He gave clear direction at 2:30 (Priya to the junction, he takes the upper fork, he checks the bottom fork) but is waiting rather than building. Collaboration looks better than visit 1. Impact is not yet visible. He is the one who needs to deliver the upper fork and the tail.

Next visit: does the top line reach the junction, is the fork built and joined, is the overlap resolved, and is Tom contributing?"}

{"self_assessment": "Impact
I built the bottom-line stretch of the fish early, then laid the back line from the middle out to the tail junction and carried it into the upper fork, which completed the picture. The finished outline is a clear fish: a nose, a curved back and belly, and a forked tail. By my inspection, all 131 standing dominoes were connected to the start.

Execution
I worked steadily and in sequence. I traced my strokes from the pad, inspected the run twice, once mid-build and once after the upper fork was laid, and confirmed that nothing was loose and that the only open ends were the two tail tips. I flagged the doubled section on the back, checked that it was still connected, and chose not to touch it, which avoided adding bump risk. I used no more dominoes than the table had.

Collaboration
I offered to take the back-to-tail stretch when I saw I was free, and told Priya she could stay put or help Maya. I asked Leo to check the gaps around the middle of the back, and he did. After the build I proposed that everyone keep their hands off the table, and the team agreed to that.

Leadership
I took the initiative on the tail-junction stretch and the upper fork without being asked. I gave clear status updates to the table and set the hands-off rule before the push. That kept the table coordinated and protected the finished piece until the push.", "my_share_percent": 35}

{"self_assessment":"Impact
I put up the initial fish sketch on the pad, which gave the table a shared shape to build from: one line over the back, one under the belly, and a forked tail, all flowing from the nose. At the final check, all 131 standing dominoes were connected to the start and would fall, so the judge should see a clear fish outline.

Execution
I inspected the table at several points (the nose split, the tail junction, the middle of the back) to confirm the lines were connected as they grew. I flagged the doubled-up spots on the back and confirmed they stayed connected, so nothing needed redoing. I also reported when the bottom line was complete out to the tail fork, which let the others focus on the slower top line. I kept my hands off once the fish was done, to avoid bumps.

Collaboration
I gave out the work so people weren't crowding each other: Priya went to help the top line, Maya was moved to the middle of the back so she and Priya weren't on top of each other, and Tom took the tail stretch and upper fork. I backed Maya's fish idea early so we could start building quickly, and I agreed with the hands-off plan near the end.

Leadership
I kept the table's focus on the slowest part, the top line, and suggested re-splitting the work when two people were overlapping. I helped coordinate the join points between lines and the order of the build, and I supported the decision to stop touching the table before the push.

Overall, the table delivered a complete, connected fish. My part was the sketch, the checks and the coordination, and I believe it contributed meaningfully, though Maya, Tom and Priya laid most of the dominoes.","my_share_percent":25}

{"self_assessment": "Impact
I took on the top line of the fish, which was the slowest stretch to build. I offered to carry it from the end of the existing run onward toward the tail, and I laid about fifteen dominoes extending it over the back. That helped it reach the tail junction so the whole fish could join up. At our final check, all 131 standing dominoes were connected to the start, and the table agreed the picture read clearly as a fish.

Execution
I worked quietly and steadily on my own stretch. I inspected the run closely early on, again mid-build, and once more near the end. These checks were to confirm that the joins on the top line were sound and that nothing was loose. When the build was complete I kept my hands off the table, because bumps were the main risk.

Collaboration
I offered to take the slow top line when I saw it was falling behind. I confirmed with Maya which end I should pick up from so we wouldn't work on top of each other. I suggested she move out toward the tail so we weren't crowding the same spot. I stayed clear of Tom's upper fork and Leo's tail work, and I offered help there if anyone wanted it. I also backed the team's decision to leave the table alone once it was finished.

Leadership
I saw where the build was bottlenecked and volunteered for it without being asked. I proposed a clear split of the work and kept the team informed about what I was doing. I supported the agreement to stop touching the table so the result would stay intact.

Overall, I contributed a real, well-placed share of the top line and helped with checking, in a team effort that produced a complete, connected fish.", "my_share_percent": 20}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I proposed the big-fish concept in the first seconds of the round: a nose start, one line over the back and one under the belly, and a forked tail. The table adopted it, and it suits the medium because the outline alone says 'fish'. I laid the start domino at the nose and the first stretch of the top line. Before the push, the run was connected from the nose to both tail tips, with about 131 of 131 dominoes falling by eye.

Execution: I worked from the sketch so the shape matched the plan. I laid the start and the first stretch of the top line, then moved to the middle of the back when the table needed to parallelise. I used several close inspections of the run to confirm that the chain was connected and that the only open ends were the tail tips. Once the fish was complete, I recommended keeping hands off the table to avoid bump damage, and I kept to that myself.

Collaboration: I kept the table informed throughout. I assigned the top line, bottom line and tail early so everyone had a job from the start. When Priya offered to take the far stretch of the top line, I accepted straight away and pointed to where the line ended so she could continue from it. I moved out of her way to avoid crowding, and I backed Tom on the upper fork. I stayed responsive to suggestions and kept messages short and clear.

Leadership: I set the direction quickly with a simple, buildable idea and divided the work so several people could build in parallel. I called the hands-off decision once the run was verified, and I reminded the table of the time with the two-minute call. I kept the team calm and energised, and the plan stayed on track to the push.", "my_share_percent": 35}
